bounded_statement: For the selected result in results/report.md (two-sample Student t test, t(46) = 7.56, p < 0.001, significant at alpha = 0.05), the workflow entered all 48 gauge readings as separate observations into scipy.stats.ttest_ind, even though the declared independent unit is piling_id and each of the 12 pilings contributes four correlated depth-band readings. The reported degrees of freedom (46) and p-value therefore rest on an independence assumption the data violate; the correct unit-level test on 12 piling means yields t ≈ 4.00 with 10 degrees of freedom (p ≈ 0.003). The issue is bounded to the inflated precision of the selected result: the direction and significance of the coating difference survive unit-level reanalysis.

counterevidence_considered.description: The workflow does compute piling-level aggregates and the report presents a piling-means table, showing the unit structure was acknowledged descriptively; a correct t test on those 12 piling means (coal_tar_epoxy: 54.4, 58.4, 60.4, 62.4, 66.4, 72.4 vs glassflake_polyester: 40.4, 44.4, 46.4, 50.4, 52.4, 56.4) still gives t ≈ 4.00, df = 10, p ≈ 0.003, so the directional conclusion of a significant coating difference is robust to fixing the unit of analysis — the inflation affects the reported precision (t, df, p), not the sign of the finding.
counterevidence_considered.observed_value: unit-level reanalysis: t ≈ 4.00, df = 10, p ≈ 0.003 (still significant at alpha = 0.05)

evidence.description: The input data confirm four highly correlated rows per piling: readings within a piling decline smoothly with depth and cluster tightly around the piling's own level (e.g., PIL-01 spans 50.4-58.4 while PIL-11 spans 66.4-77.4), so within-piling readings are not independent draws.

extensions.x-stage1-falsification-attempt: I tried to defeat the finding three ways. (1) Could the test actually have run on piling means rather than readings? No: the code passes by_coating arrays (24 elements per coating) to stats.ttest_ind, computes df = a.size + b.size - 2, and the report shows t(46) on 48 readings — df 46 is only possible with 24+24 rows, not 6+6 pilings. (2) Could the four rows per piling be plausibly independent, making row-level entry legitimate? No: the data description states all four readings from a piling share its coating, position, and exposure, and the CSV shows tight within-piling clustering (each piling's four readings span roughly 8 um/yr while piling means span 54.4-72.4 within one coating group), indicating strong within-unit correlation. (3) Could fixing the unit of analysis overturn the finding of an issue? I recomputed the test on the 12 piling means: pooled variance 36.8, standard error 3.50, t ≈ 4.00, df = 10, p ≈ 0.003. The conclusion's direction survives, but this does not falsify the issue — the issue class concerns repeated entry of the same independent unit into a row-independent procedure, which demonstrably occurred and inflated the reported t from ~4.0 to 7.56 and df from 10 to 46.

root_cause: workflow/analysis.py groups corrosion rates by coating_system only (by_coating = bucket(records, lambda r: r[GROUP_COL])) and passes those reading-level arrays of 24 values each directly to stats.ttest_ind, a procedure that treats every array element as an independent observation. The four depth-band readings from each piling — which the data description says share the piling's coating, berth position, and exposure — are thereby each entered as if they were separate independent units, quadrupling the effective sample size (48 rows vs 12 pilings) and inflating the degrees of freedom from 10 to 46. The script computes by_piling aggregates but uses them only for a descriptive table, never for the test.
